why_how.text: Knowing the three credential types tells you which card a situation calls for, from an ID card to a full license.
Federal agencies accept only Real ID-compliant cards, so the star decides whether your card works at an airport checkpoint.

scenario.text: Jordan has an older, non-compliant Indiana license and a flight coming up, and is renewing the license next month.

reasoning.text: A non-compliant card can be upgraded during a renewal if Jordan brings original or certified documents for identity, lawful status, Social Security number and residency.

result.text: Jordan brings the four kinds of documents to the renewal and leaves with a starred, Real ID-compliant card for the checkpoint.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any valid Indiana license gets you through a TSA airport checkpoint.

correction.text: Federal agencies such as DHS and TSA accept only Real ID-compliant licenses and ID cards, which carry the star.

memory_support.text: Star in the corner, cleared for federal doors.

prompt.text: Your Indiana license has no star in the upper right corner. Will TSA accept it at an airport checkpoint?

answer.text: No. Without the star it is not Real ID-compliant, and TSA accepts only compliant cards.

rationale.text: The star marks compliance, and federal agencies accept only Real ID-compliant licenses and ID cards.

lines.text: One star that matters for federal use.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on Indiana credentials. Before you can drive, it helps to know what the Bureau of Motor Vehicles actually hands out. There are three kinds of credentials, and each fits a different stage of life on the road. Then there is Real ID, the federal standard that decides whether your card can get you through an airport checkpoint or into a secure federal building. By the end of this lesson you will be able to name the credential types, read what a card is telling you at a glance, and explain how a card becomes Real ID-compliant.

lines.text: ID cards, learner's permits, driver's licenses.
Permit category includes motorcycle and commercial permits.

narration.text: The Indiana BMV issues three kinds of credentials: identification cards, learner's permits and driver's licenses. Each of the last two is really a family. The learner's permit category covers the driver, motorcycle and commercial learner's permits, while the license category covers the driver's license and the commercial driver's license. One cost rule is worth remembering. An identification card costs nothing for a person who is already eighteen, or who will turn eighteen on or before the next General or Municipal Election. So a high school senior about to vote can get an ID card at no charge.

title.text: Reading a card at a glance

lines.text: Star in the upper right: Real ID.
Older designs stay valid until expiry.

narration.text: Indiana cards carry visual clues. A credential for a resident under twenty-one uses a vertical layout and prints the dates on which the holder turns eighteen and twenty-one, which makes age checks quick. A star in the upper right corner shows that the card is Real ID-compliant and can be used as identification for federal purposes. Indiana began issuing redesigned credentials with new security features in twenty nineteen, but older cards are not thrown away. An older card remains valid until the expiration date printed on it, so you do not need a new card just because the design changed.

lines.text: Federal minimum standards since two thousand five.
DHS and TSA accept only compliant cards.

narration.text: The federal Real ID Act of two thousand five set minimum standards for state credentials so that compliant cards can be used for federal purposes, such as boarding commercial flights or entering military bases and other secure federal sites. Indiana has met the Real ID requirements since January first, twenty ten. Here is the practical rule. Federal agencies such as the Department of Homeland Security and the Transportation Security Administration accept only Real ID-compliant licenses and ID cards for entry to federal facilities, and that includes TSA airport checkpoints. A card without the star will not do that job.

lines.text: Upgrade at renewal, amendment or replacement.

narration.text: If your card is not Real ID-compliant, you can upgrade it during a renewal, an amendment or a replacement, using original documents or certified copies. For the upgrade, your branch visit must include documents proving four things: your identity, your lawful status, your Social Security number and your Indiana residency. Photocopies are not enough. The full list of acceptable Real ID documents is in Appendix A of the manual and on the REALID.IN.gov website, and the BMV also has a toll-free phone line. Plan the visit so you bring every category at once and avoid a second trip.

lines.text: Trap: a valid license is not always accepted.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers assume that because their license is valid, it works everywhere. For driving in Indiana, a valid license is fine. For federal purposes it is a different story. Federal agencies such as DHS and TSA accept only Real ID-compliant licenses and ID cards, so a valid card without the star can be turned away at an airport checkpoint. A second trap is the design. A redesigned card is not automatically Real ID, and an older card is not automatically invalid. Look for the star to answer the federal question, and look at the expiration date to answer the validity question.

Here is a quick check: your Indiana license has no star in the upper right corner, and you are flying next week. Will TSA accept it at the airport checkpoint? Use the two rules from this lesson. The star is what shows that a card is Real ID-compliant, and federal agencies such as TSA accept only compliant licenses and ID cards. So the answer is no. To fix it, you could upgrade at a renewal, amendment or replacement by bringing original or certified documents for identity, lawful status, Social Security number and residency. If you said yes, review what the star means.

lines.text: Upgrade with four kinds of proof.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. Indiana issues identification cards, learner's permits and driver's licenses, and the permit and license families each include several kinds. An ID card is free once you are eighteen or will be by the next election. A vertical card means the holder is under twenty-one, and a star in the upper right corner means Real ID. The federal Real ID Act set the standards, Indiana has been compliant since twenty ten, and federal agencies accept only compliant cards. To upgrade, bring proof of identity, lawful status, Social Security number and residency at your next renewal, amendment or replacement.

why_how.text: Only legal residents can get an Indiana credential, so residency comes before any application.
New residents face fixed deadlines, and the testing they need depends on how long their old license has been expired.

scenario.text: Rae moves to Indiana with an out-of-state license that expired seven years ago.

reasoning.text: Because the license has been expired more than five years, the knowledge-only path does not apply.

result.text: Rae must pass both a knowledge exam and a driving skills test, and she should start within her sixty days as a new resident.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a never-licensed newcomer can simply get a license within sixty days.

correction.text: A new resident who never held a license elsewhere must hold an Indiana learner's permit for one hundred eighty days first; the sixty-day deadline is for getting the license.

memory_support.text: Sixty to switch, one-eighty to learn, five years splits the tests.

prompt.text: A new resident's out-of-state license expired three years ago. Which exams are needed?

answer.text: A knowledge exam only, because the license expired less than five years ago.

rationale.text: Under five years expired means a knowledge exam; over five years adds a driving skills test.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on moving to Indiana. If you are new to the state, three questions decide your path. Are you a legal Indiana resident? How long do you have to switch to an Indiana license? And which tests will you face, given the license you bring with you? The answers depend on details such as whether you were ever licensed before and how long ago your old license expired. By the end of this lesson you will be able to sort a newcomer into the right path and name the deadline and the exams that path requires.

lines.text: Indiana home, Indiana voter, or Indiana-school dependent.
Students and temporary workers are not residents.

narration.text: Only legal Indiana residents can obtain an Indiana credential. Residency can be shown by keeping an Indiana home address without claiming another state, by being registered to vote in Indiana, or by having a dependent enrolled in an Indiana elementary or secondary school. Some people living here are not treated as residents for credential purposes. That includes college students and active-duty service members who do not claim Indiana residency, temporary employees, and anyone who does not intend Indiana to be a permanent home. So presence alone is not residency; intent and ties to the state matter.

lines.text: Sixty days to get the license.
Never licensed: permit for one hundred eighty days.

narration.text: Indiana residents may hold only one credential at a time, even when the other came from another state. If the BMV finds that you already hold a credential from another state, territory, DC or Puerto Rico, that card must be surrendered before your Indiana application is processed. Now the deadlines. A person who becomes an Indiana resident has sixty days to get an Indiana driver's license. A new resident who has never held a valid license in another state must first hold an Indiana learner's permit for one hundred eighty days before applying for a license. Keep sixty for switching and one hundred eighty for learning.

lines.text: Bring the license, the record or a letter.
Under five years expired: knowledge exam.
Over five years: knowledge plus skills.

narration.text: A new resident aged eighteen or older with a valid out-of-state license brings one of three items: that license, a copy of the official driving record, or a verification letter. Testing depends on the old license. A knowledge exam is required when it expired less than five years ago or has been held unrevoked for less than one year. When it has been expired for more than five years, you must pass both a knowledge exam and a driving skills test. Applicants under eighteen face extra rules: they must be older than sixteen years and one hundred eighty days, have held the license at least one hundred eighty days, and pass a knowledge exam and a vision screening.

Here is where newcomers slip. The sixty-day rule and the one-hundred-eighty-day rule sound similar, but they answer different questions. Sixty days is how long a new resident has to get an Indiana license. One hundred eighty days is how long a newcomer who was never licensed elsewhere must hold an Indiana learner's permit first. A second trap is the five-year line. An out-of-state license expired less than five years means a knowledge exam, while one expired more than five years means a knowledge exam plus a driving skills test. Ask which clock the question is about before you pick a number.

Here is a quick check: a new resident brings an out-of-state license that expired three years ago. Which exams are needed for the Indiana license? Use the five-year line. A license expired less than five years ago calls for a knowledge exam, and only a license expired more than five years adds the driving skills test. Three years is under five, so the answer is a knowledge exam. The applicant still has the sixty-day deadline to get the Indiana license and must surrender the old credential. If you picked both exams, revisit where the five-year line falls.

lines.text: Show residency and keep one card.

narration.text: Let us wrap up the move. You must be a legal Indiana resident, shown by an Indiana home, Indiana voter registration or a dependent in an Indiana school, and students or temporary workers who do not claim Indiana are not residents. You may hold only one credential, so any other state's card is surrendered. You have sixty days to get an Indiana license, but if you were never licensed elsewhere you first hold a permit for one hundred eighty days. Adults bring their license, record or a verification letter, and how long the old license has been expired decides whether you need one exam or two.

why_how.text: The learner's permit is the first step to a license, and its requirements change with your age.
Practice driving is legal only with the right supervisor in the front seat, and the allowed supervisors depend on the permit holder's age.

scenario.text: Ty is seventeen with a learner's permit and wants to practice with his twenty-two-year-old licensed cousin.

reasoning.text: A relative supervising a permit holder under eighteen must be at least twenty-five with valid driving privileges; only a licensed spouse may be as young as twenty-one.

result.text: The cousin is too young, so Ty practices with his thirty-year-old aunt who holds a valid license.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any licensed adult relative can supervise a permit holder under eighteen.

correction.text: A relative must be at least twenty-five and hold valid driving privileges; a younger licensed spouse at least twenty-one is the only exception.

memory_support.text: Relative twenty-five, spouse twenty-one, permit two years.

prompt.text: Ana is twenty with a learner's permit. Can her licensed coworker, aged thirty, supervise her practice drive?

answer.text: Yes. A permit holder eighteen or older may practice with any validly licensed driver at least twenty-five.

rationale.text: For adult permit holders the supervisor need not be a relative; age twenty-five and a valid license are what count, or a licensed spouse at least twenty-one.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on ID cards, learner's permits and practice driving. This is the stage where most new drivers begin. You will see who can carry an Indiana ID card and how a fifteen-year-old can add a motor driven cycle endorsement. Then you will learn what it takes to get a learner's permit at sixteen or older, and what extra steps apply before sixteen. Finally, you will learn how long a permit lasts and exactly who may sit beside you while you practice, because the allowed supervisors change with your age. Take it one stage at a time.

An identification card can be issued to an Indiana resident of any age who does not hold a driver's license. An ID card holder who is at least fifteen and passes an MDC knowledge exam receives an MDC endorsement on the card and may then operate a motor driven cycle. Both the identification card and the MDC endorsement are valid for six years. There is one exception: cards for lawful temporary residents expire on the end-of-stay date instead. So the ID card is more than identification for a young rider who passes the MDC exam.

lines.text: Sixteen or older: documents, vision, knowledge exam.
Under sixteen: at least fifteen plus enrollment proof.

narration.text: At sixteen or older, you get a learner's permit by proving identity, lawful status, Social Security number and residency with Appendix A documents, and by passing a vision screening and a knowledge exam. If you are under sixteen, you must also be at least fifteen and show a Certificate of Driver Education Enrollment from a BMV-licensed behind-the-wheel provider, dated no more than three weeks before the class starts. A certificate of completion from an online theory course is not accepted as that proof. Any permit applicant younger than eighteen must also name an emergency contact who is at least eighteen.

lines.text: ID card and MDC: six years.
Expired over one hundred eighty days: retest.

narration.text: A learner's permit is valid for two years from the issue date, except that permits for lawful temporary residents end on the end-of-stay date. Compare that with the six years an identification card and an MDC endorsement last. If you let a permit lapse, watch the calendar. Renewing a learner's permit that has been expired for more than one hundred eighty days requires retesting, which means taking the knowledge exam again. The good news is that any time you spent holding a valid permit still counts toward the one-hundred-eighty-day holding period, so the earlier practice time is not lost.

lines.text: Under sixteen in driver education: instructor or specialist.
Under eighteen: relative twenty-five, spouse twenty-one.

narration.text: A permit holder under sixteen who is enrolled in driver education may drive with a licensed driver training instructor or a BMV-recognized certified driver rehabilitation specialist in the front passenger seat. A permit holder under eighteen may practice with a relative by blood, marriage or legal status who is at least twenty-five with valid driving privileges, or with a licensed spouse at least twenty-one. Teens not in driver education may also use a school instructor or a rehabilitation specialist, and teens in Department of Child Services care may use a licensed driver at least twenty-five whom the Department approves. At eighteen or older, any licensed driver at least twenty-five, or a licensed spouse at least twenty-one, qualifies.

Here is the trap. It is tempting to think any licensed relative can ride along. For a permit holder under eighteen, a relative must be at least twenty-five and hold valid driving privileges. Only a licensed spouse may be younger, at twenty-one or older. A twenty-two-year-old licensed cousin does not qualify. The opposite trap catches adults. A permit holder aged eighteen or older does not need a relative at all; any validly licensed driver who is at least twenty-five will do, or a licensed spouse at least twenty-one. Check the permit holder's age first, then the supervisor's age and relationship.

Here is a quick check: Ana is twenty and holds a learner's permit. Her licensed coworker, who is thirty, offers to supervise a practice drive. Is that allowed? Start with Ana's age. Because she is eighteen or older, the rule for adults applies, and adults may practice with any validly licensed driver who is at least twenty-five, or with a licensed spouse at least twenty-one. The coworker is licensed and thirty, so yes, the drive is allowed. The relative requirement applies only to permit holders under eighteen. If you said no, review how the rule changes at eighteen.

lines.text: ID card at any age without a license.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. An ID card goes to any resident without a license, lasts six years, and can carry an MDC endorsement from age fifteen. A permit at sixteen or older needs documents, vision and a knowledge exam, while under sixteen you must be at least fifteen and show behind-the-wheel enrollment, not an online certificate, and anyone under eighteen names an adult emergency contact. A permit lasts two years, and more than one hundred eighty days expired means retesting. Supervisors must be at least twenty-five, or a licensed spouse at least twenty-one, with special options for driver education students.

why_how.text: Every applicant must clear the vision screening, so knowing what to bring and what happens on a failure avoids surprises.
The knowledge exam is the main test of this guide, and knowing who must take it and its timing rules keeps a branch visit from being wasted.

scenario.text: Jade reaches the branch twenty minutes before closing, hoping to take the computer-based knowledge exam that day.

reasoning.text: To test the same day you must arrive at least thirty minutes before the branch closes.

result.text: Jade has arrived too late for a same-day exam, and if she later fails, she waits until the next business day to retake it.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a failed knowledge exam can be retaken right away the same day.

correction.text: After a failure you must wait until the next business day to retake the knowledge exam.

memory_support.text: Thirty minutes early, one business day to retry.

prompt.text: A driver is renewing an Indiana license with seven active points on the record. Is a knowledge exam part of the renewal?

answer.text: Yes. Six or more active points means the knowledge exam is required at renewal.

rationale.text: The points rule adds the knowledge exam for renewing drivers with six or more active points on the Indiana record.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on the vision screening and the knowledge exam. These are the two checks that stand between you and a learner's permit, and they also come back for some renewals. You will learn who must pass the vision screening and what to do if you wear glasses or contacts, what the knowledge exam is built from, which applicants must take it, and the timing rules that decide whether you can test today or must come back tomorrow. Knowing these details saves you a wasted trip to the branch. Both checks happen at a branch, so plan the visit.

Every permit or license applicant, including renewals, must pass a vision screening unless eligible to renew online. If you wear glasses or contact lenses, say so and wear them for the screening. Failing the branch vision screening can lead to further evaluation. Even if you bring a letter from your own doctor, Driver Ability may still require more testing. So the safest plan is simple: bring and wear whatever corrective lenses you normally drive with, and expect that a failed screening is the start of a review rather than the end of the matter.

lines.text: Permit applicants and some new residents.
Licenses expired over one hundred eighty days.
Six or more active points at renewal.

narration.text: The knowledge exam is a multiple-choice test drawn from Indiana law, defensive driving practices and this manual, and it expects you to read regulatory, warning and traffic signs and signals. It is required for permit applicants, for new residents whose out-of-state license is expired or who hold an out-of-country license, for new residents under eighteen with an out-of-state license, and for residents whose Indiana license expired more than one hundred eighty days ago. A driver renewing with six or more active points must also take it, as must certain military renewals after long absences. The BMV also offers separate knowledge exams for CDL endorsements and for motorcycle, MDC and for-hire operation.

lines.text: Failed? Return the next business day.

narration.text: Here is the trap that wastes trips. You cannot walk in at the last minute and expect to test. To take the computer-based knowledge exam the same day, you must arrive at least thirty minutes before the branch closes. The second rule is about failure. If you fail, you cannot simply try again a few minutes later; you must wait until the next business day to retake the exam. Do not confuse these rules with the driving skills exam, which is booked in advance. For the knowledge exam, think arrival cutoff and next-business-day retake.

Here is a quick check: a driver is renewing an Indiana license and has seven active points on the Indiana record. Is the knowledge exam part of this renewal? Recall the points trigger. A driver renewing a license with six or more active points must also take the knowledge exam. Seven is more than six, so yes, the exam is required. Points are only one trigger; a license expired more than one hundred eighty days is another. If you thought points only matter for suspensions, remember that they also bring the knowledge exam back at renewal time.

lines.text: Thirty minutes early, next day to retry.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. Every applicant passes a vision screening, wearing glasses or contacts if they use them, and a failure can lead to further evaluation even with a doctor's letter. The knowledge exam is multiple choice, drawn from Indiana law, defensive driving and the manual, including signs and signals. Permit applicants take it, as do certain new residents, residents whose license expired more than one hundred eighty days, and renewing drivers with six or more active points. Arrive at least thirty minutes before closing to test the same day, and after a failure wait until the next business day.

why_how.text: Knowing where you may take the skills exam and how to book it keeps the final step of licensing on schedule.
The examiner can reject an unready vehicle, so preparing the car is part of passing.

scenario.text: Max booked a BMV skills exam two weeks ahead and arrives with his family's car, which has a cracked mirror, and his mother wants to ride along.

reasoning.text: The examiner may reject a vehicle with broken glass or mirrors, and only the examiner or other BMV staff may ride during the exam.

result.text: Max should fix the mirror before the date, show current registration, and his mother waits outside.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every camera in the car must be switched off for the skills exam.

correction.text: Only interior cameras must be off for the whole exam; backup cameras are allowed.

memory_support.text: Book within three weeks, bring a ready car, ride alone.

prompt.text: Your test car has an interior dash camera and a backup camera. Which may stay on during the skills exam?

answer.text: Only the backup camera; the interior camera must be off for the whole exam.

rationale.text: The rule bans interior cameras during the exam but allows backup cameras.

title.text: The last step to a license

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on the driving skills exam, the final step for most new drivers. You will learn where the exam can be taken, including at a participating driver training school, and which applicants must instead test with a BMV examiner. You will see how far ahead a BMV exam can be booked, what the vehicle must have, who may ride along and which cameras may run. Finally, you will learn how the examiner scores the drive, so you know exactly what is being watched from the passenger seat. Each rule here is simple once you see it laid out.

lines.text: Course of thirty hours theory, six behind the wheel.
Result valid until the permit expires.
Course failure sends you to a branch.

narration.text: A permit holder can take the driving skills exam at a participating BMV-licensed driver training school after finishing a course of thirty hours of theory and six hours behind the wheel, and that result stays valid until the permit expires. Schools may give the skills exam to any holder of a valid Indiana learner's permit, whether or not the permit carries driver's education restriction J. The exam must be taken at a BMV branch instead if the student fails either part of the driver education course, or if the school does not take part in the skills test program.

title.text: When a BMV examiner must test

lines.text: Some young transfers and out-of-country licenses.
Indiana license expired over five years.

narration.text: Some applicants must take the skills exam with a BMV examiner rather than at a school. That includes new residents under eighteen who held an unrevoked out-of-state license for at least one hundred eighty days but less than one year, and new residents holding an out-of-country license. A BMV skills exam is also required when an Indiana license has been expired more than five years, when a BMV restriction requires testing, or when a medical complaint or the medical board leads the BMV to require an evaluation. In these cases, plan on booking the exam directly with the BMV.

lines.text: Book three weeks to forty-eight business hours ahead.
You bring a legal, insured, safe, clean car.

narration.text: A BMV driving skills exam can be booked no more than three weeks and no less than forty-eight business hours in advance. You supply the vehicle, and the BMV charges nothing for the exam. The car must be legally equipped, insured, safe and clean, and you must show its current registration before the exam. The examiner may reject a vehicle that is not properly registered or has unsafe tires, a missing bumper, broken glass or mirrors, or a door that does not work. During the exam, only the BMV examiner or other authorized BMV staff may ride in the vehicle.

lines.text: Interior cameras off; backup cameras allowed.

narration.text: Here is a trap with two parts. First, cameras. Interior cameras must be switched off for the whole skills exam, but backup cameras are allowed, so you do not need to disable the camera that helps you reverse. Second, passengers. Parents, friends and supervising drivers do not ride along; only the BMV examiner or other authorized BMV staff may be in the vehicle. Students often get one half of each rule right and the other half wrong. Remember interior off, backup fine, and the examiner rides alone with you. Check both before the exam day.

Here is a quick check: your test car has an interior dash camera and a backup camera. Which one may stay on during the skills exam? Apply the camera rule. Interior cameras must be switched off for the whole exam, while backup cameras are allowed. So the backup camera may stay on, and the interior dash camera must be turned off before you start. While you are getting the car ready, also make sure it is registered, insured, safe and clean, with working doors, mirrors and tires. If you switched both off, remember backup cameras are allowed.

Let us finish with scoring. The examiner does not teach during the exam. After asking a few required questions, the examiner scores your drive objectively on a standardized form. Scoring covers lane use and signaling, keeping a safe gap to the vehicle ahead, holding your speed and leaving room when being passed, speed control, defensive habits, following instructions, and approaching intersections with a full stop when one is required. Put it together: test at a participating school or book a BMV exam within the window, bring a ready car, ride alone with the examiner, and drive the way you practiced.
